know ive been tweeting about this a lot but really think papertrade could be a generational setup

high leverage perps are crypto's most profitable product to date, demand for speculation is not going to go away

ability to open/close synthetic 1000x positions w/ no market impact is a novel mechanism, paired w/ the house-trader relationship where trader losses fund the onchain LP, & all losses after a certain LP cap get paid out to traders staking the platform's native paper token - can see how this can maintain traction longterm, already at 50M+ paid out to $PAPER stakers in first week

every other perp dex's revenue comes from a small take rate on the fees of volume, no perp dex has been able to monetize directly trader losses, of which it's been shown is a much larger number, in theory winners should be able to easily get paid out from house LP over time as high leverage has a difficult success rate, ideal state is that its closer to 50/50 winners/losers after a certain LP cap and even then its a much better model allowing traders to own the house

what's more interesting tho is that the model should be able to be extensible to other games outside of just perpetual futures, the online gambling industry is massive, and none of the online casinos are +EV for users, every major online casino is -EV as thats how the house makes money by creating games that are slightly better probabilistically for the house and monetizing losses over time, with papertrade it should be possible to let people speculate on other similar games with the same model as losses going back directly to paper stakers instead of just to the house - so im curious to see what team is thinking of here

if hyperliquid is the AWS of all of finance, then papertrade could be the AWS of all high leverage speculation money games on the internet, will be cool to see how the next several months play out, dont think people have gone deep enough on the possibilities with one of the first novel onchain experiments in awhile that also rewards its most active participants

Papertrade advertises zero fees. I went through the numbers on a simple trade and that isn't what I found.

Say you go long Bitcoin at $80,000 with $1,000 of margin at 1000x. Your position is worth $1M, or 12.5 Bitcoin.

Each $1 move in Bitcoin is $12.50 to you. Your $1,000 covers an $80 drop, so your margin runs out at $79,920.

Papertrade liquidates you at about $79,960. That is a $40 drop. At that point you have lost $500 on paper, but they keep the full $1,000.

On the winning side, say Bitcoin goes up $50 to $80,050. Your profit on 12.5 Bitcoin is $625. Papertrade pays you $406, which is 35% less.

Here is what they pay at different move sizes:

A $25 move earns $312 and pays $157. That is a 50% cut.

A $50 move earns $625 and pays $406. That is a 35% cut.

A $100 move earns $1,250 and pays $940. That is a 25% cut.

A $200 move earns $2,500 and pays $2,032. That is a 19% cut.

A $500 move earns $6,250 and pays $5,333. That is a 15% cut.

A $1,000 move earns $12,500 and pays $10,843. That is a 13% cut.

The cut gets smaller as the move gets bigger, but it never goes away.

At 1000x most trades end on small moves, because Bitcoin moves $40 or $50 all the time. Small moves are where the cut is largest.

Putting the two sides together, a $40 drop costs you $1,000 and a $50 rise pays you $406. To break even on those terms you need to be right about 71% of the time.
For comparison, Hyperliquid would charge roughly $900 in taker fees to open and close a $1M position. That fee is stated up front. Your margin also runs all the way to zero before you are liquidated.

On Papertrade the cost comes from the early liquidation and the reduced payouts on wins. Each one shows up in the price you get rather than as a fee. Combined with 1000x leverage, it puts the odds well against the trader.

🚨 🇺🇲 The US bond market is starting to say the trillions of dollars promised to build its infrastructure could become impossible to finance under current conditions and I think we are witnessing a genuine regime shift.

📊 For three years, markets have rewarded companies announcing the most spectacular investment plans, but now investors are finally starting to ask the right questions. Who is financing these projects? At what cost? With what guarantees? For what return? 47 major data center projects have been delayed, canceled, or blocked in 2026, while only 35% of the US data center pipeline is actually credible according to Bernstein. We are talking about a potential investment wave exceeding $10 trillion between 2025 and 2032 - FT

📉 Companies developing these infrastructures must spend billions upfront to purchase GPUs, build data centers and secure electricity supplies, while the associated revenues may not materialize for several years. Their entire business model depends on their ability to keep raising capital at reasonable costs, but that assumption is currently being challenged. CoreWeave lost 25% last week while some of its bonds suffered a sharp sell-off as the market is wondering whether these projects are financially viable at all.

➡️ Few other examples to understand. Cipher agreed to absorb the first $359 million in cost overruns on one project, creating an additional equity requirement of $750 million. Nscale has a contract potentially worth $45 billion with Anthropic but Anthropic can walk away if certain financing or delivery commitments are not met. Meanwhile, SB Energy needs around $174 billion in capital to fulfill contracts representing $430 billion in future revenue, despite not having completed a single data center. Some companies are being valued on enormous contracts without having demonstrated that they can actually finance and deliver the infrastructure behind them.

⚠️ We also need to revisit the circular financing structure of this industry which I have discussed before. Nvidia invests in companies that buy its chips, AI labs sign contracts that allow developers to raise debt, and SPVs or private credit funds finance infrastructure based on expected future revenues. As long as capital keeps flowing, the system works, but if investors suddenly demand much higher yields, the entire mechanism can start breaking down. Projects get delayed, GPU orders are postponed, developers face financial difficulties, and creditors reassess their exposure. A financing crisis can trigger an investment crisis before demand for AI even starts slowing down and many people tend to forget that. Moreover, that risk is concerning given how important AI-related investment has become as a driver of US economic growth.

📈 I do not think we are witnessing the collapse of the entire industry. Instead, we may be entering a much more brutal selection process between financially viable projects and those built on unrealistic assumptions. Lower Fed rates will not solve the problem as if credit spreads widen faster than risk-free rates decline, the overall cost of financing will continue to rise.

💸 I maintain that we need to return to a cost of capital and valuation levels that are consistent with the actual economic profitability of these projects. The technological success of AI does not guarantee financial success for the companies funding its infrastructure. History has already taught us this through railroads, telecommunications, and the internet. A technology can revolutionize the economy while destroying enormous amounts of investor capital.

The current tensions in the bond market are a serious warning sign ⚠️

📉 Companies developing these infrastructures must spend billions upfront to purchase GPUs, build data centers and secure electricity supplies, while the associated revenues may not materialize for several years. Their entire business model depends on their ability to keep raising capital at reasonable costs, but that assumption is currently being challenged. CoreWeave lost 25% last week while some of its bonds suffered a sharp sell-off as the market is wondering whether these projects are financially viable at all.

Nscale has a contract potentially worth $45 billion with Anthropic but Anthropic can walk away if certain financing or delivery commitments are not met. Some companies are being valued on enormous contracts without having demonstrated that they can actually finance and deliver the infrastructure behind them.

Nvidia invests in companies that buy its chips, AI labs sign contracts that allow developers to raise debt, and SPVs or private credit funds finance infrastructure based on expected future revenues. As long as capital keeps flowing, the system works, but if investors suddenly demand much higher yields, the entire mechanism can start breaking down. Projects get delayed, GPU orders are postponed, developers face financial difficulties, and creditors reassess their exposure. A financing crisis can trigger an investment crisis before demand for AI even starts slowing down and many people tend to forget that. Moreover, that risk is concerning given how important AI-related investment has become as a driver of US economic growth.

📈 I do not think we are witnessing the collapse of the entire industry. Instead, we may be entering a much more brutal selection process between financially viable projects and those built on unrealistic assumptions. Lower Fed rates will not solve the problem as if credit spreads widen faster than risk-free rates decline, the overall cost of financing will continue to rise.

💸 I maintain that we need to return to a cost of capital and valuation levels that are consistent with the actual economic profitability of these projects. The technological success of AI does not guarantee financial success for the companies funding its infrastructure. History has already taught us this through railroads, telecommunications, and the internet. A technology can revolutionize the economy while destroying enormous amounts of investor capital.

The current tensions in the bond market are a serious warning sign ⚠️

I shorted the market over the weekend

And then I longed it

And then I hedged

And then I closed a long at the bottom

Then I closed another long at the bottom

I am not a perps trader. I never have been. I've lost money trading perps pretty much my whole crypto career. I don't really have the discipline for it, and I struggle to implement and stick to systems.

I get carried away by narratives, and by emotions. I know all of this.

So the way I do my perps trading is to set aside ~1% of my total portfolio and treat it as gambling money. For some reason, I get a lot more invested (emotionally, intellectually) about how my tiny perps positions are doing and it distracts me from worrying or caring about my longer term spot positions.

So yeah I lost a few thousand dollars doing random shit on perp dexes this weekend, but it prevented me from touching my conviction bags and it entertained my wee little degenerate gambling mind.

Highly recommend segmenting your portfolio and having your long term holds and spot positions (and cash) in one basket, and your gambling positions in another - for leverage, for meme coins, for whatever you want to FOMO in or out of.

Kudos to all the great traders out there who can profit through volatility, but I am more of an investor than a trader, and I know my strengths and weaknesses, and am content with staying in my lane.

Tampered Ledgers drained $91M+ from hundreds of wallets, plus a $141M lawsuit, a data breach and a bunch of wind-downs.

Here's all the damage from the past week in one post:

• Some Ledgers sold through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis had a hidden implant that stole recovery phrases during setup. $91M+ gone. Buy direct from the manufacturer.

• DWF Labs affiliates are suing BitGo for $141M, claiming it sold discounted FF and ESPORTS tokens about two months before their lock-up ended.

• A breach of Based's card dashboard exposed cardholders' names, passport/NRIC numbers and addresses, tied to their wallets. Expect scammers who already know your name.

• Blur's frontend shuts down November 12. The protocol stays live onchain, and $BLUR keeps the fee switch.

• Relay is retiring its Vaults. Withdraw through the app by December 31, or straight from the contracts after that.

• Edgen, an AI copilot for crypto and stock investors, shut down October 12. Accounts are closed and its X account is suspended.

The XRPL bug is the one I keep thinking about. It sat in the code for ten years and an AI agent found it first… luckily a whitehat.

The "Mythos risk" is real, and I'm not sure every protocol makes it through. The ones that do are gonna come out a lot stronger.

Ultimately, precompiles and EVM are both the wrong place to put most cryptography support into Ethereum. The reason is that precompiles and EVM both operate on data that has to be included into the ethereum chain somehow, which realistically means included in a block as calldata. That space is limited - even with PeerDAS and blocks-in-blobs, there's a practical cap of ~8 MB/s before it starts getting uncomfortable.

Remember: it's not a blockchain. It's a cryptographic world computer. Any data/computation that does not need to be in the "main thread" of data/execution should not be put into the main thread.

Instead, the correct solution is... EIP-8288 maximalism.

If you have any heavy computation that's self-contained, compute it and STARK it client-side (this is quickly getting faster and faster, even on phones), and push the STARK through the EIP-8288 recursive aggregation mechanism. The chain sees the fact that the computation was done and what the result is; it never needs to see the actual data and computation.

This way everyone can use whatever cryptography they want, the Ethereum chain can be lean, and we never need to add more precompiles again.

Hello, friends,

There’s nothing like a Sunday for discussing current market conditions. And that’s exactly what we’re going to do today.

When we encounter a difficult situation, we like to categorize it.

For example, is this a problem that money can solve? Or, more relevant to the current situation, can we learn something from it and draw useful lessons?

That is what we’ll explore here.

The world’s leading pharmaceutical and biotech analyst is Umer Raffat, who works in New York for Evercore ISI.

As we do every weekend, we listened to his weekly podcast. This time, he opened with the topic of fund performance.

Here are a few things we learned.

First, the chaos in fund performance is not limited to biotech. According to ISI, technology funds are also going through a difficult and chaotic period.

This suggests that the current situation may also be connected to rising interest rates, in addition to the performance of $MRNA, a subject we have discussed extensively before.

Within biotech, ISI reports that market-neutral funds are down approximately 2% this year, while long-biased funds are down by double digits, except for a few fortunate funds that held stocks involved in M&A transactions.

Just how chaotic is the situation?

We have already seen junk stocks, led by $MRNA, skyrocket.

At the same time, large pharmaceutical stocks have rallied strongly, benefiting from a flight to safety.

The DRG index has gained approximately 15% over the past year and around 4% since the beginning of October.

To illustrate the chaos, we asked Claude to examine the 13F filings of the 25 largest dedicated healthcare hedge funds and identify their 25 most popular holdings.

We then asked Claude to chart the performance of these stocks this year.

The results show a 32.3% decline over the past month and a half.

Making matters worse, many healthcare funds also held significant short positions in stocks that surged dramatically, including $MRNA, $GRAL, $TWST, $IOVA, $NTRA, and others.

Naturally, this intensified the pain.

So, is the lesson to avoid popular stocks?

Not necessarily.

Even high-quality, attractively valued companies outside the market consensus have experienced aggressive selling.

It appears that investors have been selling quality stocks to chase speculative biotech names and large pharmaceutical companies.

One important lesson is that hedging through the $XBI ETF, which has substantial exposure to speculative biotech stocks, has provided relatively little protection against this particular market rotation.

What happens next?

One way to evaluate the opportunity is through forward valuations.

Using projected 2031 earnings, certain high-quality biotech companies appear to trade at significant discounts to the broader pharmaceutical industry.

In times like this, if you're a long term investor, you don't want to be waffling about being in or out, you want to be stacking units systematically. Don't get confused by the traders, it's a separate game.

On unit accumulation, depending on how long you've been in the game, it's helpful to think in "relative units" of the investment you did best with. I'll use $ETH because the math is easy and relates well to younger networks. 

ETH has ~120M units. Let's say I once held 10 ETH.

Now I'm looking to stack $SOL, but SOL has ~636M units, or ~5.3x the # of units. Therefore, to have an equivalent position size in network terms, I'd need 53 SOL. If I want to own double the network % of SOL, that I owned of ETH, I'd need 106 SOL.

Or, perhaps I'm considering $TIA, which has ~1.16B total supply, or ~9.7x the # of units of ETH. In that case, I'd need 97 units of TIA to have a network equivalent. If I want to place a bigger network bet on TIA, because the network value is lower than when I entered ETH, then 10x the % ownership would require me to accumulate 970 TIA. 100x the % ownership = 9,700 TIA. Going for significantly more ownership, at cheap prices, if you're right, can lead to asymmetric outcomes.

$ZEC is another good example of this, since its supply mirrors $BTC's. And so it's easy to think of your "dream # of BTC," and aim to accumulate that in ZEC, if you're so inclined.

Pick your networks of choice, and do the math. I have always found thinking in unit terms keeps me grounded, optimistic, and goal oriented in dreary times. I can then dream about future upside in the thick of the bull, but the important thing is to systematically stack the units with a high conviction methodology in the bear or early-bull pullbacks. 

In terms of where we are now, which is probably why most of you are still reading :) BTC has been bleeding out the long-tail while remaining resilient, with many names 20-40%+ down from the highs while BTC is down just shy of 10%. You can either say BTC has already bled the risk appetite out of the market and so most of the work is done, or you can say BTC hasn't dropped much so it'll be really terrible if it goes cliff diving. I'm sympathetic to the former view. 

I read this as an early-bull opportunity rather than a warning sign that this move was a "bull trap," and so I'm inclined to be a buyer. You have to respect the possibility of lower levels, and so tranche out any dry powder that remains with % cash used corresponding to % probability those levels are the local bottom - yes, you likely end up with some excess cash if not all levels are hit, but that's okay. And don't forget, there's already opportunity in front of you.

It was important to us to have a unified supply of everything. An alternative would have been to split the supply, half digital, half physical, but then you run the risk of the weights of each becoming uneven. For instance four 1-of-1s get pulled from the digital supply while all four still exist physically, and physical becomes the clear winner for anybody looking for a pack.

We also thought it was important not to become pack insolvent. For instance if nobody wanted to rip a pack and everybody that got a digital pack decided to redeem for a physical, we are now able to process those redemptions and ship everybody their physical packs. If we had split the supply into digital and physical, then we would not be able to fill those redemption requests.
